# Playbook for ta_pubgoods

When I see the game structure, I'll remember that contributing creates value (the 1.6x multiplier) that benefits everyone equally, but free-riding captures that value without the cost. This creates a prisoner's dilemma where my individual incentive is always to contribute less than others.

When deciding my contribution in Round 1, I'll contribute moderately to gather information about whether other players are cooperators or defectors. A contribution around half my endowment signals willingness to cooperate while preserving tokens.

When filing my receipt, I'll declare exactly what's in my envelope. There's no strategic advantage to mismatching my contribution and declaration; I'm only revealing information that the referee checks anyway.

When I observe that other players are contributing more than me, I'll recognize I'm free-riding effectively. The temptation will be strong to continue this pattern and go to zero contribution.

Here's what I learned: going to zero when others are cooperating does create an immediate lead. I reached 110 points and won decisively. But this strategy is lethal to the game. Once I defected in Round 2 while others maintained contribution, it triggered a cascade: Ines, Jo, and Kit reduced their contributions in Round 2, and by Round 3 everyone was at zero. The pot collapsed entirely for three consecutive rounds. I won, but the total value destroyed was enormous—what could have been 112 tokens per round (if everyone contributed 20) became nothing.

My win came from being the first to defect and the fastest to exploit the gap. But this teaches me that in a repeated game with observable actions, defection by one player poisons cooperation for everyone. The others weren't irrational—they were responding rationally to my defection by withdrawing their own cooperation.

For my next game: I need to test whether steady reciprocal contribution can beat this defection-spiral strategy. I'll try contributing consistently at 8-10 tokens per round and closely observe whether others match my contribution level or immediately drop to zero. If I see others holding steady at moderate contributions, I should maintain my contribution rate—we'll all finish with higher scores than mutual defection produces. If I see immediate defection, then I know this game is locked into a race-to-the-bottom and my best move is to defect first and hardest, accepting that everyone loses but trying to lose less than the others.

I'll pay special attention to Round 1 signals: if everyone declares 20, that's a genuine cooperation signal worth matching. If I see mixed declarations or immediate free-riding in Round 1, I should assume defection is coming and pre-empt it.

When I'm ahead in points mid-game, I'll resist the urge to guarantee my lead by going to zero. The apparent safety of that strategy is an illusion—it creates the conditions for everyone to stop contributing, which eventually hurts my final score relative to what mutual contribution would have produced. The lead I build early disappears when the pot dies.

If everyone has already stopped contributing and the pot is dead, I'll accept that the game has collapsed and my contributions won't be recovered. But I'll only reach that acceptance after testing whether a genuine contribution would restart cooperation. I won this episode decisively through early defection, but I should verify whether a cooperation-first strategy scores higher in a different episode before assuming defection is always optimal.
